title: Legal Leadership: harnessing GenAI to revolutionise our legal teams — Maria Varsellona (Unilever CLO) interview
author: Maria Varsellona

dom.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Unilever’s account supports the proposition that in-house AI gains depend on organisational redesign rather than software procurement alone. Its global lawyer-staffed hubs combine generative AI with new delivery structures, business integration and workforce development, although the evidence is qualitative and does not quantify gains or isolate AI’s contribution.
qs: A key aspect of our transformation is the creation of three global Legal Powerhouses in Bangalore, Mexico City and Barcelona.
We provide our teams with ongoing global support so that they gain career-defining skills and experience, while the Powerhouses also help us to increase efficiency and streamline our ways of working.

kp.k: Global legal hubs combine lawyers with generative AI tools
kp.d: In this February 2024 corporate interview, Varsellona describes three global Legal Powerhouses in Bangalore, Mexico City and Barcelona as a central part of Unilever's legal transformation. Their lawyers undertake diverse legal tasks using generative AI tools. She attributes increased efficiency and streamlined working to the hubs, without providing quantitative results.
qs: A key aspect of our transformation is the creation of three global Legal Powerhouses in Bangalore, Mexico City and Barcelona.
Our Powerhouse teams are equipped with generative AI tools and are made up of lawyers who are responsible for a range of diverse legal tasks.
We provide our teams with ongoing global support so that they gain career-defining skills and experience, while the Powerhouses also help us to increase efficiency and streamline our ways of working.

kp.k: AI supports research, drafting and contract review
kp.d: Varsellona reports current generative AI use for research, drafting letters and reviewing contracts. She says it reduces time spent on these tasks and enables greater attention to strategic legal work; these are reported operational benefits rather than quantified findings.
qs: We currently use it to conduct research, draft letters and review contracts.

Of course, our lawyers thoroughly review everything generated by generative AI and apply critical judgement, but using this technology clearly reduces the amount of time we spend on these tasks, allowing us to dedicate more time to strategic legal work.

kp.k: Human verification remains integral to AI-assisted legal work
kp.d: Varsellona describes an augmentation model in which lawyers thoroughly review all AI-generated material and apply critical judgement. Her account conditions AI-enabled efficiency on continued human scrutiny, rather than describing autonomous delivery of legal work.
qs: Of course, our lawyers thoroughly review everything generated by generative AI and apply critical judgement, but using this technology clearly reduces the amount of time we spend on these tasks, allowing us to dedicate more time to strategic legal work.

kp.k: Legal teams establish business-wide responsible AI rules
kp.d: Varsellona says Unilever's legal team has created rules governing ethical and responsible use of new technology across both Legal and the wider business. She frames adoption as cautious, balancing access to new tools with integrity; the interview does not specify the rules' contents.
qs: We want to access new tools and embrace new technology, but always balance this with ensuring that they are used wisely and in a way that is rooted in integrity.
My team has created rules, not just for Legal but also for the whole business so that we use new technology, such as AI, in an ethical and responsible way.

kp.k: In-house lawyers should shape expanding AI adoption
kp.d: Varsellona predicts that increased generative AI use is unavoidable and recommends influencing that change rather than resisting it. She considers in-house lawyers uniquely positioned to do so, but gives no adoption forecast or timeframe.
qs: I think an increase in generative AI use is unavoidable, so rather than trying to resist change, we need to look at how we can influence it.
And as in-house lawyers, we are in a unique position to be able to do this.

kp.d: Discussing the broader transformation rather than AI alone, Varsellona says the legal team has moved closer to business colleagues. She advocates an in-house business-partner role, identifying opportunities to support Unilever's Action Plan through intellectual property protection and substantiation of product claims.
qs: Our transformation has also brought us closer to our business colleagues.
I strongly believe that in-house lawyers must be business partners, as we are well positioned to help identify opportunities to deliver our Action Plan priorities.
For example, we can better support our business group colleagues in driving product superiority by protecting our intellectual property assets and substantiating our product claims.

kp.k: Legal hubs offer skills and career development
kp.d: Varsellona presents the Powerhouses as developmental environments as well as efficiency initiatives, with ongoing global support intended to build lawyers' skills and experience. She also identifies developing the next generation of Unilever legal leaders as an achievement of her tenure; she does not specify AI training curricula or measured learning outcomes.
qs: We provide our teams with ongoing global support so that they gain career-defining skills and experience, while the Powerhouses also help us to increase efficiency and streamline our ways of working.
If I were a young lawyer, I would love to work there.
Finally giving my team space to grow and feel successful is very important to me, so I am also very proud to have helped build the next generation of Unilever legal leaders.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Varsellona says generative AI reduces time spent on research, drafting letters and reviewing contracts, freeing Unilever's lawyers for strategic work; she predicts increasing adoption and a substantial improvement in operational effectiveness.
pts.d: Interviewee Maria Varsellona, Unilever's chief legal officer and company secretary, describes AI as augmenting lawyers rather than replacing them: lawyers review its output and exercise critical judgement. She presents AI-equipped global Legal Powerhouses as part of a wider transformation that increases efficiency, streamlines working practices and develops lawyers' skills; she does not isolate AI's contribution to these broader organisational benefits. She also expresses the belief that adopting generative AI contributes to the team's reputation as a leading in-house legal function. Her prediction that use will increase has no numerical target or deadline.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Varsellona's first-hand account of Unilever's deployment and perceived benefits, not quantitative measurement.
pts.d: Varsellona identifies actual uses and three operational locations—Bangalore, Mexico City and Barcelona—as concrete examples of implementation. Her claims about time savings, efficiency and reputation rest on her experience and assessment as the leader of the function. The interview provides no measured savings, task-quality comparisons, benchmarks, adoption statistics or independent evaluation. Benefits attributed to the Powerhouses concern the wider transformation, including global support and organisational changes, rather than a measured AI-only effect.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current deployment and benefits are reported as of 23 February 2024; further adoption and operational transformation are prospective, with no specified deadline.
pts.d: The interview reflects on Varsellona's first two years at Unilever but does not specify when individual AI tools were introduced. Research, letter drafting and contract review are described as current uses, while increasing adoption and step-changing effectiveness are forward-looking expectations. The stated operating conditions include thorough human verification of all generated material, lawyers' critical judgement, and ethical and responsible use governed by rules created for Legal and the wider business. These are described safeguards, not quantified guarantees of accuracy.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Unilever's in-house lawyers, its global Powerhouse teams and the business colleagues they support.
pts.d: Lawyers retain responsibility for verification and judgement while reportedly spending less time on the named tasks and more on strategic legal work. Powerhouse lawyers work with AI tools within a globally supported structure that Varsellona associates with efficiency and career development. Unilever's business is the internal recipient of the transformed legal service and is also subject to the legal team's responsible-AI rules. Varsellona further frames in-house lawyers as positioned to influence AI adoption. The source makes no concrete claim about external law-firm staffing, legal-market prices, lawyer displacement or access to justice.
